lesson.title: Oxidation States: Chemistry's Electron Bookkeeping
lesson.summary: An oxidation state is a bookkeeping charge assigned to an atom in a compound to track how electrons are distributed, letting chemists follow electron transfer even in covalent bonds where electrons are shared rather than fully exchanged.
lesson.body:
Ionic compounds make electron transfer easy to see: an atom loses one or more electrons and becomes a positively charged cation, another atom gains those electrons and becomes a negatively charged anion, and the resulting charges are real, physically meaningful quantities. Covalent compounds are messier, because atoms share electron pairs rather than fully handing them over, so there is no literal charge sitting on any one atom to point to. Oxidation states solve this problem by extending the logic of ionic charge into a universal bookkeeping system that works for every compound, ionic or covalent, real charge or not.

This connects directly back to two earlier ideas. From the study of elements, recall that an atom in its pure elemental form, uncombined with any other element, has not gained or lost or shared anything relative to itself, so its oxidation state is defined as 0. Oxygen gas, O2, solid iron, Fe, and chlorine gas, Cl2, all have an oxidation state of 0 for every atom, regardless of how many atoms are bonded together, because all the atoms in each case are identical. From the study of chemical bonds, recall that electronegativity describes how strongly an atom pulls on shared electrons. Oxidation states use exactly that idea: for a covalent bond, chemists imagine, purely as a bookkeeping fiction, that the more electronegative atom in the bond gets to keep both of the shared electrons entirely, and the oxidation state is the hypothetical charge that atom would carry under that assumption. For a genuinely ionic bond, where an electron actually was transferred, the oxidation state and the real ionic charge are the same number, since sodium chloride's Na+ ion truly does carry oxidation state and charge of +1, and its Cl- ion truly does carry oxidation state and charge of -1.

Oxidation states matter because they let chemists identify, at a glance, which atoms in a reaction gained electron density and which lost it, even in reactions where nothing is a simple ion. An atom whose oxidation state increases during a reaction is said to be oxidized, since it has effectively lost some claim on electrons, and an atom whose oxidation state decreases is said to be reduced, since it has effectively gained some claim on electrons. That pairing of oxidation and reduction is the foundation of all of redox chemistry, and it only works as a systematic tool once you can reliably assign an oxidation state to every atom in a formula, which is exactly the skill the next chapter builds, one clear rule at a time.
